interview_metadata.name: Mikala Langley
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) ??? Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I grew up in Cary, North Carolina, in a pretty structured middle-class family. My parents were both big on being on time, doing your reading, writing thank-you notes, and helping at school or community events, so I was always the kid with a planner and a pencil pouch. I was shy when I was younger, but I loved books, museums, and anything where I could organize information. In high school I did National Honor Society, volunteered at the local historical society, and spent a lot of weekends at the Cary Theater or at community festivals with my family. I finished my bachelor's degree early in the humanities, focusing a lot on literature, public history, and archival work. The biggest turning point was getting involved with a campus museum exhibit, where I helped catalogue documents and build an Omeka site. That made preservation feel less abstract and more like a practical way to tell inclusive stories. I am not married and do not have children. I live at home right now while I figure out graduate school and try to build experience toward becoming an archival specialist or museum collections coordinator. I deal with anxiety, so routines like baking, yoga, gardening, and meditation are a big part of how I stay steady.

follow_ups.question: What was your house like growing up, day to day?
follow_ups.response: It was orderly but warm. Dinner was usually around 6:30, homework came before TV, and Sunday afternoons were often errands, library books, or baking something with my mom.

follow_ups.question: Who shaped your interests the most when you were young?
follow_ups.response: My mom definitely shaped my reading habits, and a high school history teacher, Ms. Garner, encouraged me to think about archives as more than old boxes. She made local history feel alive.

follow_ups.question: What do you consider your first real adult responsibility?
follow_ups.response: Coordinating part of the campus exhibit timeline. I had to track metadata, communicate with faculty, and make sure small errors did not become public mistakes.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yes. During college I had a point where I was deciding whether to follow a more general English-literature path or commit seriously to museum and archival work. I loved close reading Austen and Joyce, but I did not want my work to stay only in essays. Then I volunteered for a university museum exhibit that included regional civil-rights materials and family letters. I spent hours cataloguing, checking dates, scanning items, and writing short descriptions for the Omeka collection. It was stressful because I wanted everything to be correct, but I also felt unusually calm because the work had structure and meaning. By the end of the project, I knew I wanted a career preserving materials and helping communities interpret them.

follow_ups.question: What were the actual options in front of you then?
follow_ups.response: One option was applying to literature-heavy graduate programs eventually. Another was aiming for museum studies or library science, which felt more practical and community-facing.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone help you make the decision?
follow_ups.response: A faculty advisor and the museum coordinator helped. They told me I had the patience and attention to detail for collections work.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was partly conscious and partly gradual. I made the conscious choice to keep taking archival and public-history opportunities, but the feeling that it fit me came slowly through doing the work.

follow_ups.question: What made it feel like a real choice?
follow_ups.response: I changed the kinds of internships, classes, and faculty conversations I pursued.

follow_ups.question: What made it feel gradual?
follow_ups.response: I did not wake up with a career title in my head. I just kept noticing that cataloguing and exhibit planning made sense to me.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. More formal mentoring about museum careers would have helped. I had support, but I had to piece together information about master's programs, paid internships, and what entry-level archival jobs actually require.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: A clear checklist of credentials, sample resumes, and honest advice about unpaid versus paid experience.

follow_ups.question: Where did you get information instead?
follow_ups.response: Mostly faculty, museum websites, Reddit threads, and professional association pages.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I do not have a partner or children. My parents, Lauren and Mark Langley, are the biggest family figures in my life. My mom is a school librarian, and she is the person I talk to about books, recipes, and whether I am overthinking something. My dad works in software project management in the Research Triangle, and he is very practical and calendar-oriented, so I probably got some of my planning habits from him. I also have a younger brother, Owen, who is in high school. We are close in a teasing, sibling way. My family is supportive, but they also have expectations around education and responsibility. Living at home at 19 can feel a little like being halfway adult, but financially it is what makes sense while I plan my next steps.

follow_ups.question: How often do you spend time with your parents?
follow_ups.response: Daily, since we live together. We usually eat dinner together four or five nights a week.

follow_ups.question: What do you and your brother do together?
follow_ups.response: We watch Hurricanes games sometimes, and I help him with English papers when he asks, though he pretends not to need it.

follow_ups.question: Who do you go to when you are stressed?
follow_ups.response: Usually my mom first, then one close friend if I need someone my age.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My immediate household is my parents, my younger brother, and me. I am also close to my grandmother in Apex, and I call her about once a week.

follow_ups.question: What do you talk about with your grandmother?
follow_ups.response: Family news, her church friends, and sometimes old Cary stories.

follow_ups.question: Do you see extended family often?
follow_ups.response: Mostly holidays, birthdays, and the occasional Sunday lunch.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My closest friend is Priya, who I met in a seminar on memory and public history. We usually text daily and meet for coffee every couple of weeks. I also have a small group from yoga and one friend, Hannah, from the campus museum project. I am not dating anyone right now. My social circle is not huge, but it is steady. I prefer one-on-one plans, like tea, a bookstore visit, or a Cary Theater showing, rather than loud parties.

follow_ups.question: Where do you usually meet friends?
follow_ups.response: Coffee shops in Cary or Raleigh, the library, or sometimes the yoga studio lobby after class.

follow_ups.question: How do you keep in touch?
follow_ups.response: Mostly texting and Instagram messages. I am not a big phone-call person except with family.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Cary, in the 27511 area, in a quiet suburban neighborhood with older trees, sidewalks, and mostly single-family homes. It is very typical Research Triangle suburbia: families, commuters, good schools, grocery stores close by, and lots of people who work in tech, education, or health care. I like that I can get to the library, the Cary Theater, and downtown Cary pretty easily. Our yard is small but we have a garden patch where I grow herbs with my mom. It is not exciting in a big-city sense, but it is calm, clean, and familiar.

follow_ups.question: Where do you go most often nearby?
follow_ups.response: The library, Trader Joe's, the yoga studio, downtown Cary, and sometimes the historical society.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: A few by name. We wave, bring in packages sometimes, and chat during storms or yard work.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel very safe overall. I still pay attention if I am walking alone at night, but that is more general caution than anything specific to my neighborhood.

follow_ups.question: Do you walk around the neighborhood?
follow_ups.response: Yes, usually late afternoon or early evening, especially when I need to clear my head.

follow_ups.question: Has anything ever made you feel unsafe there?
follow_ups.response: Not really, aside from occasional car break-in posts on the neighborhood Facebook group.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is stability, access, and quiet. The downside is that Cary can feel expensive and a little socially polished, like everyone is doing fine all the time, which can make it harder to admit when you feel uncertain.

follow_ups.question: What do you like least day to day?
follow_ups.response: Driving is necessary for a lot of things, and I wish there were more easy transit options.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you attached to it?
follow_ups.response: My family, the library, the arts scene, and the fact that the Triangle has real museum and university opportunities.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is me, my mom Lauren, my dad Mark, and my younger brother Owen. My mom works as a school librarian, my dad works in software project management, and Owen is in high school. We all have pretty regular schedules. I have my own bedroom and do chores like dishes, laundry, some grocery runs, and helping with the garden.

follow_ups.question: Who is usually home during the day?
follow_ups.response: During the school year, often just me for parts of the day because my parents and brother are out.

follow_ups.question: Do household routines feel shared or separate?
follow_ups.response: Shared at dinner and chores, separate during work and school hours.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is a permanent household member.

follow_ups.question: No one staying short-term right now?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed recently?
follow_ups.response: No, our household has been stable.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Occasionally my grandmother stays overnight after family events, but that is rare.

follow_ups.question: How often would you say that happens?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a few times a year.

follow_ups.question: Does anyone else visit regularly?
follow_ups.response: Friends visit, but they do not stay overnight regularly.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No. Everyone who usually lives here is here.

follow_ups.question: No one away at college or military service?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Any long hospital stays recently?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: My weekdays are structured even though I am not working for pay. I usually wake up around 7:15, make tea, check email and job or graduate-program notes, then spend late morning reading, organizing applications, or volunteering-related tasks. Twice a week I go to gentle yoga, usually Tuesday and Thursday evenings. I bake once or twice a week, often sourdough or something precise like tart dough. Weekends are more family time, errands, maybe the Cary Theater, a Hurricanes game on TV, or helping in the garden.

follow_ups.question: What is the most fixed part of your week?
follow_ups.response: Yoga and Sunday meal planning. Those keep the rest of the week from feeling shapeless.

follow_ups.question: When do you do museum or historical society activities?
follow_ups.response: Usually one weekday afternoon or a Saturday morning, depending on volunteer needs.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I am not currently in the paid workforce. I am focusing on applications, volunteer experience, and figuring out whether to apply for a master's in museum studies or library science. I do unpaid volunteer work with local history-related projects, like sorting materials or helping with event setup. In the past I did campus museum work tied to school rather than a regular paid job. I am looking for entry-level museum, library, or archive-adjacent work in the Triangle.

follow_ups.question: What would be your ideal first paid role?
follow_ups.response: Archives assistant, collections assistant, or museum education/program support.

follow_ups.question: How many hours do you spend on career preparation?
follow_ups.response: Maybe 10 to 15 hours a week if I count applications, reading job posts, and volunteer tasks.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I help at home with chores, especially dishes, laundry, grocery lists, and keeping the family calendar updated when things overlap. I keep a reading journal and a baking notebook, which sounds intense, but it helps me remember what worked. I also do guided meditation several times a week, usually at night. If my brother has an English assignment, I sometimes read drafts for him.

follow_ups.question: What chores are specifically yours?
follow_ups.response: Tuesday dishes, my own laundry, some grocery pickup, and watering herbs when it is hot.

follow_ups.question: What do you track in your notebooks?
follow_ups.response: Books, quotes, baking hydration percentages, rise times, and what I would change next time.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest change is finishing my bachelor's and not having a class schedule anymore. At first that was freeing, then it became unsettling because I like external structure. I made myself a weekly schedule with blocks for applications, reading, exercise, volunteering, and chores. I have also been trying not to check job postings late at night because it spikes my anxiety.

follow_ups.question: When did that change happen?
follow_ups.response: This spring, after finishing my degree requirements.

follow_ups.question: What has helped you adjust?
follow_ups.response: Putting things on paper, yoga, and having small deadlines even when nobody else assigns them.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so that does not apply to me.

follow_ups.question: Do you have caregiving responsibilities for any children?
follow_ups.response: No, not regular caregiving.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with your brother's school routine?
follow_ups.response: Only occasionally with essays or rides if my parents are stuck.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My direct experiences have been limited and mostly routine. I have seen Cary police at community events and once had an officer come after a minor fender-bender near a shopping center. I have not had a frightening personal encounter. At the same time, I am aware that my experience is shaped by being white, suburban, and from a stable family.

follow_ups.question: What happened with the fender-bender?
follow_ups.response: No one was hurt. The officer took information, and my dad handled most of the insurance conversation.

follow_ups.question: Do police feel visible in your neighborhood?
follow_ups.response: Not heavily. Mostly traffic patrols or community-event presence.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Mostly school safety presentations and seeing officers at festivals. Nothing personally dramatic stands out.

follow_ups.question: Were those experiences positive?
follow_ups.response: They were neutral to positive for me, but also very controlled environments.

follow_ups.question: Have friends had different experiences?
follow_ups.response: Some friends of color have talked about being more nervous during traffic stops.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: No one in my immediate family or close friend group has been arrested as far as I know. I have not been arrested.

follow_ups.question: Any legal trouble close to your household?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Has fear of arrest affected your daily choices?
follow_ups.response: No, not directly.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I became eligible recently, so I have not voted in many elections yet. I did vote in the 2024 general election, and I plan to vote regularly. I am more likely to research school board, town council, and state races than some people my age because local decisions feel very concrete to me.

follow_ups.question: How did you prepare to vote?
follow_ups.response: I used the state board of elections site, candidate websites, and local news.

follow_ups.question: Did your family influence your voting habits?
follow_ups.response: Yes, my parents always treated voting as a responsibility, even when they disagreed on details.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would describe myself as left-of-center or progressive, but cautious about slogans that do not turn into actual policy. I care about public education, libraries, arts funding, reproductive rights, climate policy, LGBTQ rights, and making local history more honest and inclusive. I grew up in a suburban environment where politeness is valued, so I am not the loudest political person in the room. But my views have moved more clearly Democratic as I have gotten older. I also think institutions matter, even when they need reform. Museums, schools, courts, elections, and libraries only work if people actually maintain them and make them more accessible.

follow_ups.question: What issues feel most personal to you?
follow_ups.response: Education, libraries, reproductive rights, and how history is taught.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics at home?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, especially around elections. We try to keep it civil, but it can get tense.

follow_ups.question: Where do your views come from?
follow_ups.response: Family values around service, humanities classes, friends from different backgrounds, and watching state politics in North Carolina.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more explicit about racial justice, reproductive rights, and LGBTQ issues than I was in high school. Some of that came from college courses and some from listening to friends describe experiences I had not had. I used to think being informed and kind was enough. Now I think you also have to notice policies and power, not just individual attitudes.

follow_ups.question: Was there a particular class or event that affected you?
follow_ups.response: A public history class on memory and monuments affected me a lot.

follow_ups.question: Did anything move you in the opposite direction?
follow_ups.response: I have become more careful about online outrage. I want evidence and practical steps.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They have affected me significantly, especially in how I think about history and institutions. I was in my teens when the 2020 protests were happening, and it made policing and racism feel less like distant textbook issues and more like something shaping people's daily lives. As a white person from Cary, I know I have had a lot of insulation. It made me more attentive to whose stories get preserved and whose are treated as optional.

follow_ups.question: How did you first follow those events?
follow_ups.response: Through news, Instagram, and conversations with classmates.

follow_ups.question: Did it affect your archival interests?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it pushed me toward community-centered exhibits and regional civil-rights history.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think about them as connected to both present policy and historical memory. Policing is part of it, but so are housing, schools, monuments, archives, and whose pain gets believed. I do not think I am an expert, so I try to listen and read more than perform certainty. But I do think the core issues are real and not something people should dismiss because the conversation is uncomfortable.

follow_ups.question: What have you read or watched on the subject?
follow_ups.response: Articles from local news, museum panels, and assigned readings on public memory and race.

follow_ups.question: What feels hardest to talk about?
follow_ups.response: Defensiveness, especially with people who hear systemic racism as a personal accusation.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I have been thinking about race as something embedded in ordinary systems, not just dramatic moments. In North Carolina, you can see layers of history everywhere if you actually look: plantations, universities, suburbs, school boundaries, highways, and memorials. I also think about how easy it is for people like me to treat diversity as an aesthetic value rather than a redistribution of attention and resources. That is something I am trying to be honest about.

follow_ups.question: Does that show up in your daily life?
follow_ups.response: Mostly in what I read, which museums I support, and how I think about exhibit labels.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss race with family?
follow_ups.response: Yes, carefully. My parents are open, but generational habits still show up.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with friends and family, attended a campus discussion, donated small amounts when I could, and tried to choose research topics that take marginalized histories seriously. I have not been a major protest organizer.

follow_ups.question: Did you attend any protests?
follow_ups.response: I attended one peaceful campus gathering, but not repeated street protests.

follow_ups.question: What felt most actionable for you?
follow_ups.response: Reading, conversations, donations, and changing how I approach historical interpretation.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My close friends are mostly supportive of racial justice conversations, though people vary in how active they are. Priya is more outspoken than I am online. My parents are sympathetic but more cautious and sometimes worry about polarization. My brother mostly gets information through school and social media, so his views are still forming. Overall, the people closest to me do not dismiss the issues, but they respond in different registers.

follow_ups.question: Has this caused conflict?
follow_ups.response: A little, especially with extended relatives, but not major conflict in my immediate family.

follow_ups.question: Who influences you most on this topic?
follow_ups.response: Friends of color, public historians, and local educators.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Physically I am generally healthy. I do gentle yoga twice a week, walk in the neighborhood, and try to eat balanced meals, though I bake a lot. The main health issue for me is anxiety. It is manageable, but it affects sleep, decision-making, and how much I ruminate about the future. I use routines, mindfulness, and occasional counseling support to keep it from taking over.

follow_ups.question: Do you take any regular medication?
follow_ups.response: No regular prescription medication right now.

follow_ups.question: How often do you exercise?
follow_ups.response: Yoga twice a week, plus walks a few times a week.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easier because I live in a safe area, have access to groceries, and my family has health insurance. It is harder when I lose structure or compare myself to other people. Anxiety can make me either over-plan meals and routines or avoid things completely. Yoga helps because it is scheduled but not competitive.

follow_ups.question: What foods do you usually rely on?
follow_ups.response: Soup, eggs, yogurt, vegetables, bread I bake, and simple pasta.

follow_ups.question: What tends to disrupt your health habits?
follow_ups.response: Application stress, poor sleep, and too much scrolling.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: No major physical diagnosis, broken bone, or serious illness in the past two years. The main thing was recognizing that my anxiety was more than normal student stress during my final year of college. I had a few periods of insomnia and stomach tension when deadlines stacked up. I talked with a counselor through school and built a more consistent routine around sleep, yoga, and reducing late-night work.

follow_ups.question: Did you receive a formal diagnosis?
follow_ups.response: I was told it was generalized anxiety symptoms, though I am careful about not over-medicalizing every stressful week.

follow_ups.question: What symptoms do you notice first?
follow_ups.response: Tight chest, stomach fluttering, repetitive checking, and trouble falling asleep.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Anxiety can slow me down, especially with applications or big decisions. It has not made me unable to function, but it can make ordinary tasks take longer because I double-check everything.

follow_ups.question: What tasks are most affected?
follow_ups.response: Emails, applications, and anything where I worry about making a bad impression.

follow_ups.question: What helps you get through those tasks?
follow_ups.response: Timers, checklists, and asking one trusted person to review something.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Not in a crisis way. My grandmother has normal aging-related appointments and some joint pain, and my parents are starting to pay more attention to cholesterol and blood pressure. It makes me aware that I am getting older too, even though I am only 19, because family roles shift gradually. I sometimes go with my grandmother to errands, but I am not a primary caregiver.

follow_ups.question: Who handles most family health logistics?
follow_ups.response: My mom usually does, especially for my grandmother.

follow_ups.question: Does it create stress for you?
follow_ups.response: A little anticipatory worry, but not daily pressure.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We are fortunate because my family has insurance through my dad's job. I have not had to forgo necessary care. The hard part is more about scheduling, finding mental health providers with availability, and feeling comfortable asking for help. When I used campus counseling, access was easier but limited in number of sessions.

follow_ups.question: What kind of care is hardest to access?
follow_ups.response: Mental health care, mostly because of waitlists and finding a good fit.

follow_ups.question: Who helps with insurance details?
follow_ups.response: My dad understands the plan best, and my mom handles appointments.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Nothing like indigenous or formal non-Western medicine. We use pretty ordinary informal things: herbal tea, stretching, heating pads, yoga, meditation apps, and honey-lemon when someone has a sore throat. I see those as comfort and prevention, not replacements for medical care.

follow_ups.question: Do you use herbs from your garden that way?
follow_ups.response: Mint and thyme sometimes, mostly in tea or soup.

follow_ups.question: Would you choose alternative care over a doctor?
follow_ups.response: No, not for something serious.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I am 19, so I do not legally drink, and drinking is not part of my coping. During tough times I am more likely to bake, take a walk, do yoga, text a friend, or make tea. Sometimes I cope less perfectly by scrolling too much.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever tried smoking or vaping?
follow_ups.response: No, it has never appealed to me.

follow_ups.question: What is your most common stress habit?
follow_ups.response: Checking my phone and rereading emails too many times.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not use marijuana or other substances. I use ordinary over-the-counter medicine like ibuprofen for cramps or headaches, but not as emotional coping. My most recent experience was probably taking ibuprofen for a headache after a bad night's sleep. For anxiety, I rely on counseling tools, breathing exercises, and routine rather than medication at this point.

follow_ups.question: Have you considered anxiety medication?
follow_ups.response: I would consider it if symptoms became harder to manage, but I have not started any.

follow_ups.question: Any substance use in your close circle that affects you?
follow_ups.response: No, not closely.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: We use my dad's employer health insurance. My parents pay premiums and copays, and I am still on their plan. We budget for dental visits, prescriptions if needed, and routine checkups. I know that puts us in a privileged position because I do not have to choose between care and rent.

follow_ups.question: Do you contribute to health costs?
follow_ups.response: Not regularly. My parents cover them right now.

follow_ups.question: Are costs stressful for your family?
follow_ups.response: They are annoying, but not unmanageable.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am pro-vaccination. I got routine vaccines and COVID vaccines, and I see vaccination as a community responsibility as well as personal protection.

follow_ups.question: Did you have any hesitation?
follow_ups.response: Not really, beyond normal nervousness about side effects.

follow_ups.question: Does your family agree?
follow_ups.response: Yes, my immediate family is vaccinated and generally trusts medical guidance.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: I trust my doctor, the CDC, local public health information, and major medical centers like UNC or Duke Health. I also listen to my mom because she is careful about sources. I avoid getting vaccine information from random TikTok or Facebook posts unless I can trace it back to a reliable medical source.

follow_ups.question: Do you read scientific papers directly?
follow_ups.response: Not usually for vaccines. I rely on medical summaries from reputable institutions.

follow_ups.question: What makes you distrust a source?

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope I am in or finished with a master's program in Museum Studies or Library Science and working in a real archival or collections role in the Research Triangle. I would like to have my own apartment or share a quiet place with a roommate, and I want to be financially more independent. I hope I still bake, read, go to yoga, and stay close to my family, but with more adult boundaries. Professionally, I want to help create exhibits that make regional history more inclusive and accessible. Personally, I want my anxiety to be something I manage, not something that quietly makes all my decisions.

follow_ups.question: Where would you most like to work?
follow_ups.response: A university archive, local museum, public library special collections, or historical society in the Triangle.

follow_ups.question: What future trip do you hope for?
follow_ups.response: Florence for Renaissance art or Kyoto for gardens, if I can save enough.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value care, accuracy, and meaningful continuity. Care means showing up for people in practical ways. Accuracy matters because stories can be distorted when details are handled carelessly. Continuity means preserving what should not be lost, whether that is family recipes, local history, friendships, or a quiet routine that keeps me grounded. I also value kindness, but not the kind that avoids hard truths.

follow_ups.question: What is one object that represents those values?
follow_ups.response: My reading journal, because it is personal, organized, and full of things I do not want to forget.

follow_ups.question: What value did your parents emphasize most?
follow_ups.response: Responsibility.
